title: Prevalence and Determinants of Normocalcemic Primary Hyperparathyroidism: A Cross-Sectional Analysis of a Community Cohort
content: Background/Objectives: Normocalcemic primary hyperparathyroidism (NCPHP), characterized by elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) and normal calcium, is considered an early phenotype of primary hyperparathyroidism (PHP), but community-based prevalence data are scarce and heterogeneous. The objectives of this study were to determine the prevalence of NCPHP and other phenotypes related to calcium and PTH metabolism, as well as to evaluate potential associated clinical and biochemical variables. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of a community cohort of 1,747 adults from urban and rural areas of the Department of Cauca, Colombia, recruited by non-probabilistic sequential sampling. Participants with conditions or medications known to affect calcium-PTH metabolism were excluded. We measured PTH, ionized calcium, 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25OH Vit-D), phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), and defined nine phenotypes by cross-tabulating PTH and calcium categories. Predictors of NCPHP were identified with multivariable logistic regression. Results: The median age was 52 years, and 58.2% of participants were women. The prevalence of NCPHP was 9.8% [95% confidence interval (CI): 8.5–11.3], and classic PHP was found in 0.2% (95% CI: 0.1–0.6). In the multivariable model, only older age [adjusted odds ratio (OR): 1.02 per year; 95% CI: 1.01–1.03] and a 25OH Vit-D level <20 ng/mL (adjusted OR: 2.59; 95% CI: 1.69–3.97) independently predicted NCPHP; sex, origin, body mass index, and renal function did not. A 25OH Vit-D threshold of 23.3 ng/mL best discriminated PTH elevation (area under the curve, 0.598). Conclusions: In this large, community-based cohort, NCPHP was substantially more prevalent than previously reported, whereas classic PHP remained rare. Older age and vitamin D deficiency were the only independent correlates of the normocalcemic phenotype, findings that warrant confirmation in longitudinal studies.
